thread.title: Apple's Reliance Upon Cirrus Over the past many years, Apple

author: Patient Tech Investor
title: Apple's Reliance Upon Cirrus Over the past many years, Apple
text:
Apple's Reliance Upon Cirrus Over the past many years, Apple's ( AAPL ) reliance upon Cirrus Logic ( CRUS ) for high quality sound technology has been long and significant. What does Apple pay? What does Apple get? How important is Cirrus' technology? These are some of the questions on which we intend to provide perspective. Understanding this relationship is critical. Cirrus investors are first and foremost interested in Cirrus' heavy reliance on Apple revenue (75%). Apple depends upon Cirrus' superior differentiating technology. Most important, the sometimes very painful experience of owning Cirrus with its discounted price comes largely from what many believe is a overreliance of Cirrus upon Apple. 
Apple values high-quality sound. Its first smaller product, the iPod, sold because these products provided small-sized, higher-quality sound with simplified operation at very reasonable prices. In the late 1990s, Steve Jobs noticed a gap between PCs and pocket-sized music boxes. After about a year of development, Apple released its first iPod. It took advantage of the company's Mac music store, opening music purchases for the new pocket devices. Several models were built during the next 6 years, all of which used a Wolfson Microelectronics audio codec. The early iPods dominated the market.
With the advent of the 6th generation iPod Classic and the 2nd generation iPhone, Cirrus Logic replaced Wolfson, primarily because Cirrus offered Apple a huge technical advantage: a codec that eliminated two large physical capacitors. Apple was interested in further miniaturizing the design and those physical devices were a major obstacle. During the early years, Cirrus continued its hardware advancement by integrating more passive parts into its codec, further providing Apple with opportunities to continue miniaturizing its products. More recently, Cirrus developed codecs with significantly greater hardware/software power for adding functionality, such as always-on (AWO). In 2012, Apple added Cirrus' first digital amplifiers into their iPhone and other devices. Apple continues to use Cirrus' codecs and amplifiers in almost all of its products; Maxim amplifiers are used in the tablet line. It is critical to remember that Apple relies heavily upon sound for differentiating its products.
